name: The Coupon Collector's Problem
statement: To collect all of a set drawn at random, expect to need about n times the log of n draws.
statementAccent: n times the log of n draws
meaning: The coupon collector's problem asks how many random draws it takes, on average, to collect at least one of every kind when each draw yields one of n kinds uniformly at random. The answer is n times the nth harmonic number, which for large n is close to n times the natural logarithm of n. The surprise is that finishing a set takes far more draws than the number of kinds, because the last few are so hard to get.
mechanism: Split the collection into stages by how many distinct kinds you already hold. When you have all but a few, most draws are duplicates, so the wait for each new kind grows. With k kinds still already collected, the chance the next draw is new is the fraction still missing, and the average wait is its reciprocal. Summing these waits gives n times one plus a half plus a third and so on, the harmonic sum, which grows like the logarithm of n. The final missing kind alone takes about n draws on its own, so the endgame dominates the total.

examples.text: To roll all six faces of a fair die at least once takes about 14.7 rolls on average, far more than six, because the last faces are slow to appear.
Collecting a full run of trading cards or stickers gets disproportionately hard near the end, when almost every pack is a duplicate.
In software, the same maths estimates how many random inputs are needed before every case has been exercised at least once.

variants.name: The Erdos-Renyi limit
variants.text: Beyond the average, the time to complete the set follows a Gumbel distribution in the limit, sharpening the coarse harmonic-number estimate into a full distributional law.

variants.name: Unequal odds
variants.text: When the kinds are not equally likely, completing the set takes strictly longer than the uniform case, since the rare kinds dominate the wait.

whyItMatters: It is a canonical example in probability of geometric waiting times and the power of linearity of expectation, and it recurs across computer science in randomized algorithms, hashing, sampling, and test coverage, as well as in the everyday economics of collecting cards, stickers, and prizes. It captures a broadly useful intuition: gathering the last few items of any randomly drawn set is far costlier than gathering the first many.

working.lead: Expect n log n, not n
working.text: budget for about n times the logarithm of n draws to complete a set of n kinds, well above the number of kinds.
anticipate that the final few kinds dominate the effort, since duplicates crowd out new kinds near the end.
treat the tidy result as the easiest case, and expect longer waits when some kinds are rarer than others.

limits: The clean result assumes uniform, independent draws with replacement; unequal probabilities make completion strictly harder and require a different formula. The variance is large, of the order of the square of n, so individual outcomes scatter widely around the average. It is a proven mathematical result, but its earliest historical attribution is uncertain and it is best described as a classical result, with the sharp distributional limit credited to Erdos and Renyi.
misreadings: Completing a set of n kinds does not take about n draws; it takes roughly n times the logarithm of n, substantially more, and the multiplier grows with n. The difficulty is not evenly spread; the last kind alone costs about n draws on average, so nearly all the effort is in the tail. And the neat formula is the best case, holding only when every kind is equally likely.
origin: A classical result in probability, with the harmonic-number expectation elementary and long known, and the limiting distribution established by Paul Erdos and Alfred Renyi around 1961; earlier related analysis goes back to Laplace and de Moivre.
